opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's changed a lot. Early on I evaluated a place mostly by its mission: are these people working on the problem I think matters most? That still matters enormously, but I've learned it's not sufficient.

The first thing I look at now is whether the environment lets me think in public, or at least out loud. A lot of my most useful work has come from writing down half-formed views, having people poke holes in them, and iterating. If a place is too cautious, where everything has to be polished and pre-approved before it leaves your head, I don't do my best thinking there.

Second, I pay much more attention to feedback loops. Research on things like AI timelines or risk is really hard to get feedback on. The world won't tell you you were right for years. So I ask: who will tell me when I'm wrong? Are there colleagues who disagree with me and will actually say so, and not just defer because I've written a long report? Intellectual diversity within a small team turns out to be really valuable and surprisingly rare.

Third, I think about the gap between what an organization says it values and what it rewards. Lots of places say they want people to change their minds, to flag uncertainty, to work on the most important thing even if it's unglamorous. But you learn a lot by watching what happens to the person who says, "I think our main project is less important than we assumed." Do they get thanked or quietly sidelined?

And finally, a more personal one: sustainability. When you think the stakes are as high as I do with AI, it's very easy to burn yourself out, and some environments subtly encourage that. I've come to value places where people take the problem seriously but also treat it as a marathon, because I think this is going to be a long, weird stretch, and we need people who can keep thinking clearly through it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the environment affects where she does her best thinking and whether she can sustain her work, but does not clearly state that it can make a transformative difference to her experience of a job.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses difficult environments and AI-related burnout, but does not mention concerns about effective altruism or say those concerns trouble her more in a difficult working environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest shift for me is that I used to evaluate a working environment mostly in terms of the mission and the object-level work. Like, is this organization working on the thing I think is most important, and is the specific project I'd be doing well-targeted at that thing? And those still matter a lot to me. But I've come to put much more weight on a few things that are harder to see from the outside.

One is epistemic culture. How do people here actually update? When someone makes a prediction and it turns out wrong, what happens? Is there a norm of going back and saying "okay, I said this would take six months and it took two years, what does that tell me?" Or does everyone just quietly move on? I've found that the places where people are willing to be wrong out loud, and where being wrong isn't socially punished, are the places where I actually learn things and where the work gets better over time. And it's really hard to assess that from a job posting. You have to talk to people and ask them about specific instances.

The second thing is something like the incentive gradient you're going to be sitting in. I think I was pretty naive early on about how much your environment shapes what you end up believing. If you're at a place where everyone's livelihood depends on a particular product shipping, or on a particular narrative about timelines being true, it's just really hard to think clearly about whether that narrative is right. Not because people are dishonest, but because the pressures are subtle and cumulative. So now I ask myself, if the truth turned out to be inconvenient for this organization, would I be able to say so, and would anyone want to hear it?

And then the third thing, which is maybe more personal, is just whether the environment lets me do the slow, uncertain, kind of unglamorous work that I think forecasting and threat modeling actually require. A lot of this work involves sitting with a question for months, producing something that's mostly a list of considerations and wide confidence intervals, and having that be okay. Some environments are structured around fast, legible wins, and that's great for some kinds of work, but it's corrosive for the kind of thinking I want to do. So I look for places where there's genuine patience for that, where people value a good question as much as a clean answer.

I guess the common thread is that I've moved from asking "is this the right cause" to asking "will this environment make me a better or worse thinker over time." Because I think over a career, the second thing compounds a lot more than people expect.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a working environment shapes what she believes, whether she learns, and whether her work improves, and frames the key question as whether it will make her a better or worse thinker over time. This clearly conveys a major effect on the job experience.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention concerns about effective altruism or say that such concerns trouble her more when her immediate working environment is difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more interested in how an environment will shape my judgment, rather than just whether I agree with the people there right now. What kinds of arguments get rewarded? Can you say, “I don’t know,” or change your mind without losing credibility? If you think something important is going wrong, is there someone you can actually talk to about it?

It’s easy to imagine that you’ll bring your own values and independent thinking into any workplace and they’ll stay intact. But the people you spend time with, and what they treat as obvious or prestigious, have a real influence on you. So I’d want to look at concrete examples of how people handle disagreement and uncertainty, rather than just the organization’s stated mission. I’d be asking, “Is working here likely to make me better at noticing when I’m wrong?”

r001.rationale: The response says a workplace can shape judgment and influence values, but does not clearly state that the immediate day-to-day environment can make a transformative difference to the job experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more attentive to the feedback I’d get in a working environment. If I’m wrong about something, is someone likely to notice and tell me? And will I feel comfortable asking questions or admitting that I’m confused?

It’s easy to focus on whether the mission sounds important or the people seem impressive. But I’d also want to know what working with them actually looks like: how they make decisions, how they handle disagreement, and whether I’d have enough support to get better at the work. I’d put more weight on those day-to-day interactions than I used to.
